title: Hedwig: Dynamic Autonomy for Coding Agents Under Local Oversight
authors: Tanjal Shukla, K. J. Kevin Feng, Leijie Wang, Mohammad Rostami, Amy X. Zhang
venue: ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems (CAIS 2026), demo; arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.11495
decisions: Confirm;Act or delegate;Defer or return control
summary: Hedwig is a CLI coding agent demo that adapts its autonomy from developer interaction traces rather than static permission settings or instruction files. Hard constraints sit alongside learned behavioral guidance. An online logistic regression over 13 action features, updated by SGD after each decision and persisted per repository, scores each proposed action into silent approval, flagged approval, or live check-in. Corrections are stored as text snippets and retrieved into prompts. A synthetic-persona evaluation against Claude Code with Auto Memory shows higher recall for a cautious persona but more false positives for a permissive one. There is no user study and no transfer evaluation, so the authors frame it as a proof of concept.
relation: This is nearly a direct USIL instance: a persistent, user-conditioned autonomy policy learned from approvals across sessions. Open questions: how well do the learned guidelines generalize to new task types, and how should they handle trust miscalibration after a costly error?

title: Report on the 1st Workshop on Human-Centered Proactive and Personalized Agents for Interactive Information Access at CHIIR 2026
authors: Kirandeep Kaur, Vinayak Gupta, Tanya Roosta, Madhura Raju, Grace Hui Yang, Chirag Shah
summary: Workshop report on proactive and personalized agents for information access.
relation: Community signal for proactive personalization; useful for related-venues context.

title: To Help or Not to Help?: An Expanded Framework for Deciding Socially Appropriate Robot Assistance
summary: When robotic help is appropriate vs intrusive; social costs and human skills
relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P3; capabilities require full-text verification.

title: Towards Automating Data Access Permissions in AI Agents
authors: Yuhao Wu, Ke Yang, Franziska Roesner, Tadayoshi Kohno, Ning Zhang, Umar Iqbal
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P) 2026
summary: The paper proposes automating data-access permissions for AI agents with an assistant that learns each user's allow/deny preferences. A vignette study with 205 Prolific participants identifies the factors that shape permission decisions. A hybrid predictor combines o3-mini in-context learning on the user's own history and demographics with LightGCN collaborative filtering over other users. It reaches 85.1% accuracy overall and 94.4% at 25.9% coverage when only high-confidence predictions are automated and uncertain ones are deferred to the user. Accuracy improves with more history, but high-variance users are hard to predict. It is a proof of concept with no temporal evaluation and no external baselines.
relation: This is close to learning pi_u for confirm-vs-act from sparse approvals and rejections. Open question: does a predictor of offline decisions remain calibrated when deployed live, as preferences drift and the agent's own auto-decisions change what evidence the user gives?

title: When Should Users Check? Modeling Confirmation Frequency in Multi-Step Agentic AI Tasks
authors: Jieyu Zhou, Aryan Roy, Sneh Gupta, Daniel Weitekamp, Christopher J. MacLellan
summary: The paper asks when an agent should ask users to confirm intermediate steps in long multi-step agentic tasks. A formative study identifies a confirmation-diagnosis-correction-rollback (CDCR) pattern. The authors build a decision-theoretic dynamic-programming scheduler that places checkpoints to minimize expected user time. In a 48-participant within-subjects study against confirm-at-end, the scheduler cut completion time by 13.54% and was preferred by 81%. Gains were largest for early errors and slightly negative for late errors. Parameters are population-level and fixed. Personalization and online adaptation are explicitly deferred to future work, and time is the only cost modeled.
relation: Directly models confirmation; open question is learning the schedule per user.

title: Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents
authors: K. J. Kevin Feng, David W. McDonald, Amy X. Zhang
summary: This position paper proposes five levels of agent autonomy defined by the role the user plays: operator, collaborator, consultant, approver and observer. It treats autonomy as a design choice distinct from capability and environment. It sketches autonomy certificates for governance and assisted evaluations that assign a level from the minimum user involvement needed to reach a performance threshold. A running example illustrates each level, and open questions ask when an agent should consult or seek approval. There are no experiments, learning mechanisms or user data. Personalization appears only conceptually, as user-specified approval conditions and a possible L3 training period. It is useful as a vocabulary for procedure-level autonomy that is averaged across users.
relation: Treats autonomy as a fixed design choice; USIL asks whether it should be learned per user and context.

title: ProPerSim: Developing Proactive and Personalized AI Assistants through User-Assistant Simulation
authors: Jiho Kim, Junseong Choi, Woosog Chay, et al.
summary: Introduces a home-scenario simulation in which persona-driven simulated users rate the timing and content of an assistant's proactive suggestions. ProPerAssistant is a retrieval-augmented assistant that learns from those ratings over time, and across 32 personas it steadily improves user satisfaction.
relation: This learns per-user proactivity (when to intervene) from longitudinal feedback. Open questions: do the gains hold with real users, whose feedback is sparser and noisier than simulated persona ratings, and does it learn when *not* to intervene?

title: Proactive Agent: Shifting LLM Agents from Reactive Responses to Active Assistance
authors: Yaxi Lu, Shenzhi Yang, Cheng Qian, et al.
summary: Collects human activity data and has annotators accept or reject proactive task proposals. Those labels train a reward model that judges when an agent should initiate help. The authors also build ProactiveBench (6,790 events) and fine-tune LLMs on it, reaching an F1 of 66.47% for proactively offering assistance.
relation: This gives a learned 'when to intervene' signal from accept/reject evidence, but it is pooled across annotators. Open question: can the reward model be conditioned on a single user's acceptance history to yield pi_u for proactivity?

title: Robot Behavior Personalization from Sparse User Feedback
authors: Maithili Patel, Sonia Chernova
venue: IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (DOI 10.1109/LRA.2025.3550833); arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.19219
decisions: Act or delegate;Explain;Defer or return control
summary: TAACo personalizes a household robot's manner of assistance (do now, do later, remind, or no action) from sparse verbal feedback. GPT-4 scores abstract concepts for each task, and a per-user transformer is trained on these scores plus state variables, with attention aligned to user explanations. In interviews with five older adults (173 tasks), TAACo reached 0.71 prediction accuracy with 40 samples and 0.74 explanation accuracy, beating few-shot GPT-4 and a rule-based baseline. It generalizes to held-out tasks within each user. It does not study temporal drift, cross-user transfer, or asking decisions, and the sample is small.
relation: This directly learns user-specific 'which steps to run autonomously' with cross-task transfer from sparse evidence. Remaining questions: does it adapt online to preference drift, and does the concept representation carry over to LLM agents working in software?

title: Training Proactive and Personalized LLM Agents
authors: Weiwei Sun, Xuhui Zhou, Weihua Du, et al. (incl. Graham Neubig, Maarten Sap, Yiming Yang)
summary: The paper introduces UserVille, which turns static datasets into vague-prompt tasks with LLM user simulators holding hidden precise prompts and one of 20 interaction preferences. It also introduces PPP, a multi-objective RL method that jointly optimizes task productivity, proactivity (low user effort) and personalization (preference compliance). An agent trained on Seed-OSS-36B learns when to ask clarifying questions and how to phrase them, outperforming GPT-5 on average (+16.72), and generalizes to unseen preferences, other simulators and full SWE tasks. A 33-person user study partly confirms this but shows a sim-to-real effort gap. Personalization is preference-conditioned, not learned per user over time.
relation: Closest existing instance of training an interaction policy conditioned on user interaction preferences, but it conditions on a preference specified per episode by a simulator rather than learning it from an individual user's evidence across sessions.

title: Learning to Defer to a Population: A Meta-Learning Approach
authors: Dharmesh Tailor, Aditya Patra, Rajeev Verma, Putra Manggala, Eric Nalisnick
venue: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS 2024), PMLR 238
decisions: Act or delegate;Defer or return control
summary: Extends learning-to-defer to experts never seen in training. The system meta-learns a deferral policy that adapts at test time from a small context set describing the current expert, and an attention-based variant finds context examples similar to the test input to estimate the expert's ability more precisely.
relation: It offers a formal few-shot recipe for conditioning a defer/act policy on one human's evidence. Remaining question: it models the human's competence rather than their *preference* for control, so it is unclear how it extends to sequential agent tasks.

title: Navigating autonomy and control in human-AI delegation: User responses to technology- versus user-invoked task allocation
summary: User acceptance and perceived control depend on how delegation initiated
relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P3;P4; capabilities require full-text verification.

title: Semi-Autonomous Systems with Contextual Competence Awareness
authors: Saaduddin Mahmud, Connor Basich, Shlomo Zilberstein
venue: International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems (AAMAS 2023)
decisions: Confirm;Act or delegate;Defer or return control
summary: Extends competence-aware systems, which learn online which autonomy level to use from human feedback, to CoCAS. CoCAS handles multiple human operators whose behavior shifts over time by using Markovian context about operators and the environment, while keeping CAS's convergence guarantees. Experiments cover UAV surveillance and autonomous vehicle delivery.
relation: It is a planning-theoretic framing of adjustable autonomy learned from operator feedback, with operator drift. Open question: how would it scale to the open-ended actions and natural-language evidence that LLM agents deal with?

title: SARI: Shared Autonomy across Repeated Interaction
authors: Ananth Jonnavittula, Shaunak A. Mehta, Dylan P. Losey
decisions: Act or delegate;Defer or return control
summary: Learns shared-autonomy assistance from scratch by exploiting the fact that users repeat daily tasks. SARI recognizes the current task, reproduces the user's past demonstrations, and returns control to the human when it is uncertain, with bounded-error guarantees. Three user studies, including a pilot with a disabled user, show it matching existing methods on known tasks and beating baselines on new ones.
relation: It learns when to hand back control from one user's accumulating history. Open question: hand-back here is driven by task uncertainty rather than the user's preferred level of control.

title: Human-Robot Mutual Adaptation in Shared Autonomy
summary: This paper proposes a human-robot mutual adaptation formalism for shared autonomy. A bounded-memory model of human adaptability (BAM) is embedded in a MOMDP with a disagreement penalty. The robot maintains a belief over each user's goal and adaptability α and decides whether to guide the user toward an optimal goal or comply with their preference. In a 51-participant table-clearing study, the mutual-adaptation robot raised team performance over one-way adaptation (following the user) while keeping trust higher than a no-adaptation baseline. Adaptation is within-task only, α is fixed, the model is hand-specified, and transfer is untested.
relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P2;P3; capabilities require full-text verification.

title: The Off-Switch Game
authors: Dylan Hadfield-Menell, Anca Dragan, Pieter Abbeel, Stuart Russell
summary: The Off-Switch Game is a one-shot game-theoretic analysis of why a rational agent would allow a human to switch it off. A robot that is uncertain about the human's utility, and treats the human's off-switch decision as evidence about that utility, has a positive incentive to defer. A robot with a fixed, known reward lacks this incentive unless the human is rational. For a noisily rational human, the incentive depends on a tradeoff between the robot's uncertainty and the human's suboptimality. The paper has no learning, personalization, temporal adaptation, or empirical evaluation. It is a formal foundation for deference and autonomy decisions relevant to P3.
relation: Formal model of deference; USIL adds individual variation in desired oversight.

title: Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning
authors: Dylan Hadfield-Menell, Anca Dragan, Pieter Abbeel, Stuart Russell
summary: Formulates value alignment as a cooperative game where the robot learns the human's reward through interaction.
relation: Formal basis for learning about a human while acting; costs of querying are not user-specific.

title: Shared Autonomy via Hindsight Optimization
authors: Shervin Javdani, Siddhartha S. Srinivasa, J. Andrew Bagnell
summary: A foundational work that models shared autonomy as a POMDP with uncertainty over the user's goal, inferred from the user's input history with maximum-entropy inverse optimal control. It approximates the best action with hindsight optimization. Users finished tasks faster with less input, but their ratings were mixed, revealing a tradeoff between keeping control and finishing quickly.
relation: It is the canonical formalism for assisting under user-intent uncertainty, and its finding that some users prefer control is the motivation for USIL. Open question: how to learn each user's control-vs-efficiency preference persistently rather than hand-tuning arbitration?

authors: Eric Horvitz

authors: Ben Shneiderman, Pattie Maes
summary: Classic debate: user-controlled direct manipulation versus autonomous interface agents that act on the user's behalf.

title: Assistant or Actor? Student Trust, Control, and Delegation Regret When Using a General-Purpose AI Agent
authors: Shiva Pochampally, Shengwei An, Yan Chen
summary: A within-subjects study of 20 AI-literate CS students used a general-purpose agent on five tasks that varied in privacy, stakes and reversibility. Trust was calibrated per task: it was lowest, and approval preference highest, for the email-sending task, where the agent acted without showing a preview. Participants often rated outputs as successful yet regretted that the agent had acted without authorization, which the authors name 'delegation regret'. They argue that irreversibility plus external visibility, not stakes alone, drives trust withdrawal, and they propose an agent management layer with user-specified autonomy levels. The study is small, uncounterbalanced and single-session, and it contains no personalization or learning.
relation: Evidence that acting beyond authorization harms users even when outcomes are correct.

title: Collaborative Gym: A Framework for Enabling and Evaluating Human-Agent Collaboration
authors: Yijia Shao, Vinay Samuel, Yucheng Jiang, John Yang, Diyi Yang
summary: Co-Gym is an open framework for developing and evaluating LM agents that collaborate with humans, with dual control of task environments and non-turn-taking interaction. It supports simulated users (gpt-4o with hidden preferences) and real users (99 participants, 150 trajectories) across Travel Planning, Related Work, and Tabular Analysis. Prompted agents (autonomous, collaborative, and situational-planning) are compared on delivery, task performance, initiative entropy, and satisfaction. Collaborative agents win 66-86% against autonomous ones in the real condition. Error analysis finds failures in communication, situational awareness, and personalization. No learning occurs and adaptation stays within one session, leaving cross-session, per-user interaction learning open.
relation: Evaluates collaboration process, but not per-user adaptation.

title: Comparing Human Oversight Strategies for Computer-Use Agents
authors: Chaoran Chen, Zhiping Zhang, Zeya Chen, et al.
decisions: Ask or clarify;Confirm;Intervene or take over
summary: This paper compares four human-oversight strategies for LLM computer-use agents (Risk-Gated, Action Confirmation, Supervisory Co-Execution, Structurally Enriched) in 192 live sessions with a shared base agent and task environment. Plan-based strategies reduced the odds of problematic actions by 76%, but users blocked only 29 of 138 problematic actions that reached execution, with no reliable difference across strategies. Video coding shows that authority is often mistimed and that users check procedural correctness. The authors argue that oversight should adapt over time, but nothing is learned or personalized, and there is no transfer evaluation. It is useful as population-level evidence on procedural interaction timing.
relation: Shows that the right confirmation and intervention structure depends on context and on how recognizable risky moments are, which is what USIL's ask/act/confirm policy decides. Open question: can an agent learn per user which moments that user treats as decision-critical, instead of using one fixed oversight strategy?

title: Delegating or Doing? Understanding User Behavior in Hybrid Human-Agent Interfaces
authors: Gavin Dizon, Tyrone Justin Sta Maria, Jordan Aiko Deja, Yasuyuki Sumi
summary: This between-subjects study (N=73) compares Traditional GUI, AI-First and Hybrid modes in an LLM-augmented REST web app built with an MCP architecture, using 16 CRUD tasks. AI assistance reduced clicks, navigations and scrolling but did not change task time. In the Hybrid condition, chat use did not differ significantly by CRUD operation, yet the by-participant intercept explained about half the variance (ICC=.50), so delegation varies more across users than tasks. No model is trained and nothing is personalized; adaptive designs are only suggested. The sample is homogeneous, with a single app and model and one fixed task order, so transfer is untested.
relation: Direct empirical support for USIL's premise that delegation is a property of the user more than of the task. Open question: can an agent estimate this user-level delegation tendency from a few early interactions and adjust its own initiative to match?

title: Intuitive Programming, Adaptive Task Planning, and Dynamic Role Allocation in Human–Robot Collaboration
summary: Review of adapting plans and roles in human robot collaboration
relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P2;P3; capabilities require full-text verification.

title: Modeling Distinct Human Interaction in Web Agents
authors: Faria Huq, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Zhanqiu Guo, Venu Arvind Arangarajan, Tianyue Ou, Frank Xu, Shuyan Zhou, Graham Neubig, Jeffrey P. Bigham
summary: The paper introduces modeling human intervention in collaborative web agents. COWCORPUS holds 400 real-user trajectories (20 users, 20 tasks each) with over 4,200 interleaved human and agent actions. K-means clustering yields four interaction styles: Takeover, Hands-on, Hands-off and Collaborative. Fine-tuned LMMs (Gemma-27B, LLaVA-8B) predict at each step whether the user will intervene and outperform prompted closed models on Perfect Timing Score. Style-conditioned models generally do best on their own cluster, except Takeover. In a small user study (n=16), the deployed PlowPilot, which prompts only when intervention is likely, was rated 36.8% more useful than CowPilot. Personalization is at cluster level, with no cross-session adaptation or transfer shown.
relation: Close predecessor showing individual intervention styles; open question is adapting the agent's own policy to each style.

title: Programming by Chat: A Large-Scale Behavioral Analysis of 11,579 Real-World AI-Assisted IDE Sessions
authors: Ningzhi Tang, Chaoran Chen, Zihan Fang, et al.
summary: Analysis of about 75K developer messages from roughly 11.6K Cursor/Copilot chat sessions (899 developers, 1.3K repositories) committed to public repositories. Developers refine iteratively instead of specifying tasks upfront, delegate diagnosis, comprehension, and validation, and manage collaboration by saving plans as persistent artifacts and limiting agent autonomy through context injection and behavioral constraints.
relation: In the wild, users already encode interaction preferences by hand, as persistent plans and behavioral constraints. Open question: can an agent infer and maintain these per-user interaction rules from corrections instead of requiring users to write them?

title: Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns and Trust in LLM Agents
authors: Zhiping Zhang, Yi Evie Zhang, Freda Shi, Tianshi Li
decisions: Confirm;Act or delegate;Defer or return control
summary: A 3x3 between-subjects experiment (N=450) crosses LLM agent autonomy (none, full, risk-contingent) with personalization (none, privacy-aware, full) in message-sending scenarios using participants' real personal information. Full personalization raises privacy concern and lowers trust. Risk-contingent autonomy, where the agent hands control back to the user when a GPT-4o detector flags sensitive content, attenuates these effects, and perceived control mediates this. Full autonomy shows no significant effects. Nothing is learned: the policy is fixed, personalization is by prompting, and the study is single-session with two scenarios. It offers empirical grounding for adaptive autonomy and return-of-control design, but not per-user learning.
relation: Shows that returning control at risky moments raises perceived control, and points to a tension: the personal data USIL learns from can itself erode trust. Open question: can the triggers for returning control be learned per user while keeping user-model privacy costs acceptable?

title: Future of Work with AI Agents: Auditing Automation and Augmentation Potential across the U.S. Workforce
authors: Yijia Shao, Humishka Zope, Yucheng Jiang, et al.
decisions: Act or delegate;Defer or return control
summary: Introduces the Human Agency Scale and the WORKBank database: about 1,500 workers' preferences for automation vs. augmentation across 844 O*NET tasks in 104 occupations, paired with expert ratings of AI capability. Tasks are sorted into automation green-light, red-light, R&D-opportunity, and low-priority zones. Desired human involvement varies widely across occupations and tasks.
relation: Gives a population- and task-level prior over desired autonomy, which USIL could refine per individual. Open question: how much does a given user's preferred agency differ from the occupation/task prior, and how quickly can interaction evidence correct it?

title: Magentic-UI: Towards Human-in-the-loop Agentic Systems
authors: Hussein Mozannar, Gagan Bansal, Cheng Tan, et al.
decisions: Ask or clarify;Confirm;Act or delegate;Intervene or take over
summary: An open-source web interface for human-in-the-loop agents (web browsing, code execution, files, MCP) with low-cost interaction mechanisms: co-planning, co-tasking, multi-tasking, action guards, and long-term memory of plans. Evaluated with autonomous benchmarks, simulated users, qualitative user studies, and safety assessments.
relation: A testbed with exactly the interaction points USIL wants to personalize (plan approval, action guards, takeovers) plus cross-session plan memory. Open question: can action-guard approvals and plan edits train a per-user policy for when guards trigger and which steps run on their own?

title: Plan-Then-Execute: An Empirical Study of User Trust and Team Performance When Using LLM Agents As A Daily Assistant
authors: Gaole He, Gianluca Demartini, Ujwal Gadiraju
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI 2025)
decisions: Confirm;Act or delegate;Intervene or take over
summary: Study with 248 participants on six daily-assistant tasks of varying risk (e.g., flight booking, credit card payment). It varies user involvement in the planning and execution stages of a plan-then-execute LLM agent. Agents help when plans are good and users are involved appropriately during execution, but plausible-looking bad plans cause miscalibrated trust.
relation: Shows that the payoff from involving users at plan vs. execution stages depends on plan quality and task risk. Open question: can the agent learn from each user's history when to ask for plan or step confirmation, so trust stays calibrated without constant involvement?

authors: Hua Shen et al.

relation: Mutual adaptation framing; USIL narrows to learning per-user interaction policies.

title: Towards Optimizing Human-Centric Objectives in AI-Assisted Decision-Making With Offline Reinforcement Learning
authors: Zana Buçinca, Siddharth Swaroop, Amanda E. Paluch, Susan A. Murphy, Krzysztof Z. Gajos
decisions: Act or delegate;Suggest;Explain;Defer or return control
summary: The paper proposes offline RL to learn AI-assistance policies in AI-assisted decision-making that optimize human-centric objectives, namely immediate accuracy and learning. A tabular Q-learning policy over a 64-state space (Need for Cognition, concept, AI correctness, knowledge) selects among four assistance types. Policies are learned from data on 142 participants making exercise-prescription decisions, then tested in two new studies. Accuracy-optimized policies beat baselines for both NFC groups, sometimes achieving complementarity. Learning-optimized policies helped only low-NFC users in Experiment 1 and showed no significant effect in Experiment 2. Personalization is group-level, with a single task and crowd participants, and no transfer is tested.
relation: Closest existing example of a user-conditioned assistance policy learned with RL from interaction logs. Open question: can the policy be adapted online for a single user from that user's sparse evidence, rather than conditioned on population-level traits?

title: When to Show a Suggestion? Integrating Human Feedback in AI-Assisted Programming
authors: Hussein Mozannar, Gagan Bansal, Adam Fourney, Eric Horvitz
summary: Uses Copilot telemetry from 535 programmers to build CDHF, a decision-theoretic framework that predicts whether a suggestion will be accepted and withholds suggestions likely to be rejected, which cuts verification time and latency. Modeling the programmer's latent state improves these display decisions. Optimizing for acceptance as the reward can lower suggestion quality.
relation: A concrete case of learning when to intervene from approvals and rejections, and it warns that acceptance is a biased reward. Open question: does a policy fit on the population adapt to an individual programmer's working style and changing preferences over sessions?
