title: FSPO: Few-Shot Optimization of Synthetic Preferences Personalizes to Real Users
authors: Anikait Singh, Sheryl Hsu, Kyle Hsu, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Tatsunori Hashimoto, Archit Sharma, Chelsea Finn
summary: FSPO reframes LLM personalization as meta-learning over users: a single Llama 3.2 3B model, fine-tuned with IPO/DPO-style objectives, conditions on a user's few labeled preference pairs to infer a personalized reward and generate tailored answers. User description rationalization (RAT) and a synthetic pipeline of over 1M preferences, designed to be diverse and self-consistent, enable transfer from synthetic personas to real users. It reaches about 82-90% winrate on synthetic users and beats the base model (68%) and an SFT model (72%) in a preliminary 50-person human study. It also improves reward prediction on PRISM. It does not address interaction decisions or temporal adaptation.
relation: Strongest few-shot personalization result; remaining question is few-shot adaptation of interaction policies rather than responses.

title: Learning to Summarize User Information for Personalized Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
authors: Hyunji Nam, Yanming Wan, Mickel Liu, Jianxun Lian, Peter Ahnn, Natasha Jaques
summary: PLUS (Preference Learning Using Summarization) personalizes RLHF reward models without user IDs. A PPO-trained LLM summarizer turns each user's context, such as past conversations, into a short natural-language preference summary. A reward model conditioned on that summary predicts chosen vs. rejected responses, and the two are trained jointly. PLUS beats Bradley-Terry-Luce reward models by 11–77% on Pets and UltraFeedback and stays above 90% accuracy under topic shift. On PRISM it beats baselines for in-distribution users but not held-out users. Summaries also personalize GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 without fine-tuning (72% and 69% win rates). The work addresses output preference only: it does not model temporal drift or interaction decisions such as asking or deferring.
relation: Interpretable representation locus for USIL; could summaries capture procedural preferences?

title: Aligning LLMs with Individual Preferences via Interaction
authors: Shujin Wu, May Fung, Cheng Qian, et al.
summary: Trains LLMs with SFT and RL to infer a user's unstated preferences over a multi-turn conversation and adapt responses dynamically, using 3,310 synthetic personas and tree-structured conversations; introduces the ALOE benchmark for measuring alignment as a conversation proceeds.
relation: Studies within-conversation inference of an individual's preferences from interaction; it does not address persistence across sessions or decisions such as when to ask explicitly instead of inferring.

title: Aligning Language Models with Demonstrated Feedback
authors: Omar Shaikh et al.
summary: DITTO aligns an LLM to a user from a handful of demonstrations by treating them as preferred over model outputs.
relation: Direct policy adaptation per user; extension to procedural demonstrations is open.

title: Capturing Individual Human Preferences with Reward Features
authors: André Barreto, Vincent Dumoulin, Yiran Mao, et al.
summary: Argues that a single reward model is inadequate when people disagree, and proposes a reward-feature model that learns shared features and adapts quickly to individual raters through per-user linear weights; reports gains when preference heterogeneity is high.
relation: Gives a learning-theoretic case for per-user adaptation when disagreement is high; it leaves open how to choose evidence to gather from a user, such as when to ask, under a limited interaction budget.

title: Language Model Personalization via Reward Factorization
authors: Idan Shenfeld, Felix Faltings, Pulkit Agrawal, Aldo Pacchiano
summary: Represents each user's reward as a linear combination of shared base reward functions, so a new user can be personalized from about 10 responses, chosen by active selection; validated with synthetic users and a real human study.
relation: Few-shot, low-dimensional user weights with active query selection fit USIL's sparse-evidence setting well; it remains open whether interaction-policy preferences factor into similarly few shared bases.

title: Learning to Plan with Personalized Preferences
summary: Learns personalized planning from few demonstrations; preference based planning benchmark
relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P2;P4; capabilities require full-text verification.

title: PAL: Sample-Efficient Personalized Reward Modeling for Pluralistic Alignment
authors: Daiwei Chen, Yi Chen, Aniket Rege, Zhi Wang, Ramya Korlakai Vinayak
summary: Mixture-of-ideal-points reward model that personalizes from few samples per user.
relation: Sample-efficient per-user reward modeling over outputs; procedural preferences not modeled.

title: SynthesizeMe! Inducing Persona-Guided Prompts for Personalized Reward Models in LLMs
authors: Michael J. Ryan, Omar Shaikh, Aditri Bhagirath, Daniel Frees, William Held, Diyi Yang
summary: Induces personas from a user's interactions to build personalized reward-model prompts.
relation: Persona as representation; interaction decisions not targeted.

title: AI Alignment with Changing and Influenceable Reward Functions
authors: Micah Carroll, Davis Foote, Anand Siththaranjan, Stuart Russell, Anca Dragan
summary: This ICML 2024 paper introduces Dynamic Reward MDPs (DR-MDPs) to analyze AI decision-making when a person's reward function changes over time and can be influenced by the AI. It shows that common alignment objectives, such as real-time reward and initial reward, can incentivize undesirable influence, lock-in, or poor real-time reward, and that changing the horizon cannot reliably remove these incentives. Comparing 8 notions of alignment on toy examples, it finds each either permits undesirable influence or is overly risk-averse, with the proposed ParetoUD often reducing to inaction. The work is purely theoretical: reward functions and their dynamics are assumed known, with no user data or learning.
relation: Key reference for preference drift and influence; USIL inherits the question of which adaptation is legitimate.

title: Aligning LLM Agents by Learning Latent Preference from User Edits
authors: Ge Gao, Alexey Taymanov, Eduardo Salinas, Paul Mineiro, Dipendra Misra
summary: PRELUDE/CIPHER studies how a frozen LLM agent can learn from user edits to its outputs. The LLM infers a natural-language description of the user's latent preference from each (output, edit) pair. At test time, descriptions from the k most similar past contexts are aggregated into the prompt, so no fine-tuning is needed. In GPT-4 simulated-user summarization and email-writing environments, CIPHER cuts cumulative edit cost by 31% and 73% against baselines and has the best preference accuracy. A small human study supports this. It does not cover interaction decisions, drift, or transfer, and a gap to the oracle remains.
relation: Learns from naturally occurring edits over time; affects what is produced, not when to ask or act.

title: Distributional Preference Learning: Understanding and Accounting for Hidden Context in RLHF
authors: Anand Siththaranjan, Cassidy Laidlaw, Dylan Hadfield-Menell
summary: Shows that standard Bradley-Terry RLHF implicitly aggregates over hidden context (such as annotator identity), effectively by Borda count, and can produce bad outcomes; proposes distributional preference learning to estimate the distribution of utilities and detect hidden context.
relation: Gives the theory for why a single pooled policy fails when users differ; the open question is how to detect and resolve hidden user context online, for example by asking a question when the distributional reward shows high disagreement.

title: Diverging Preferences: When do Annotators Disagree and do Models Know?
authors: Michael JQ Zhang, Zhilin Wang, Jena D. Hwang, et al.
summary: Builds a taxonomy of why annotators disagree in human preference datasets (for example task underspecification and style), shows that Bradley-Terry reward models and LLM-as-judge collapse such divergence into a confident winner, and proposes distributional reward models that flag divergent cases.
relation: Finds that much disagreement comes from underspecification, which an agent could resolve by asking the user; the open question is whether a disagreement signal can serve as a per-user trigger for clarification.

title: Group Preference Optimization: Few-Shot Alignment of Large Language Models
authors: Siyan Zhao, John Dang, Aditya Grover
summary: Meta-learns a transformer preference module on top of an LLM that predicts a group's preferences in context from a few examples, enabling few-shot alignment to new groups without fine-tuning the base model.
relation: A few-shot, in-context meta-learning recipe that could be applied to sparse per-user interaction evidence; it is unclear whether it works at the individual level and for sequential decisions such as asking or deferring.

title: Modular Pluralism: Pluralistic Alignment via Multi-LLM Collaboration
authors: Shangbin Feng, Taylor Sorensen, Yuhan Liu, Jillian Fisher, Chan Young Park, Yejin Choi, Yulia Tsvetkov
summary: Plugs community-specific smaller LMs into a base LLM to represent diverse perspectives.
relation: Group-level output pluralism; does not address interaction decisions.

title: Personalized Language Modeling from Personalized Human Feedback
authors: Xinyu Li, Ruiyang Zhou, Zachary C. Lipton, Liu Leqi
summary: Proposes P-RLHF: a lightweight user model that learns user embeddings (explicit and implicit) jointly with the LLM from personalized preference data, extending DPO into personalized DPO that conditions on each user and handles new users.
relation: Gives a direct template for a user-embedding-conditioned policy; it remains open whether such embeddings can be learned from interaction-level signals (takeovers, interruptions) and steer when to ask or act.

title: Personalizing Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback with Variational Preference Learning
authors: Sriyash Poddar, Yanming Wan, Hamish Ivison, Abhishek Gupta, Natasha Jaques
summary: VPL personalizes RLHF by treating each user's preferences as a latent variable. A variational encoder infers a user latent z from a handful of that user's preference-pair annotations. A latent-conditioned BTL reward model and policies then adapt to the user without further training. The paper adds likelihood-based reward scaling (VPL-SPO) and active query selection that picks informative pairs, roughly halving the queries needed in simulated control. VPL beats BTL and DPL baselines on simulated control tasks and LLM reward modeling (e.g. 74.75 vs 49.84 on UF-P-2) and matches BTL on unimodal data. Users are simulated, preferences are static, and transfer is not evaluated. It is a strong outcome_individual predecessor.
relation: Latent-variable personalization for outcomes; open question is whether the same machinery can condition interaction decisions (ask/act).

title: Position: A Roadmap to Pluralistic Alignment
authors: Taylor Sorensen et al.
summary: This ICML 2024 position paper proposes a roadmap to pluralistic alignment. It formalizes three kinds of pluralistic models: Overton (a spectrum of reasonable responses), steerable (conditioned on attributes), and distributional (matching a population distribution). It also formalizes three kinds of benchmarks: multi-objective, trade-off steerable, and jury-pluralistic. A small experiment on GlobalOpinionQA and MPI finds that most post-alignment LLMs have higher Jensen-Shannon distance to human answer distributions and lower entropy than their base models, which the authors treat as initial rather than conclusive evidence. No model is trained, no individual user data is used, and interaction decisions and temporal adaptation are not addressed. It is useful framing for USIL's outcome-side and evaluation discussion.
relation: Close in genre (position paper) and in arguing against averaging; focuses on values/outputs rather than how an agent works with a user.

title: The PRISM Alignment Dataset: What Participatory, Representative and Individualised Human Feedback Reveals About the Subjective and Multicultural Alignment of Large Language Models
authors: Hannah Rose Kirk, Alexander Whitefield, Paul Röttger, et al.
summary: Collects multi-turn conversations and fine-grained ratings from 1,500 participants in 75 countries, linked to each person's sociodemographic profile and stated preferences, and documents substantial heterogeneity in preferences across individuals and groups.
relation: One of the few datasets that links individual users to their interaction-level feedback; it covers output preferences only, so it leaves open how much users differ on interaction-policy preferences such as how often they want to be asked.

title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model Is Secretly a Reward Model
authors: Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Christopher D. Manning, Chelsea Finn
summary: Optimizes a policy directly from preference pairs without an explicit reward model.
relation: Population-level objective; a common backbone for personalized variants.

title: Personalized Soups: Personalized Large Language Model Alignment via Post-hoc Parameter Merging
authors: Joel Jang, Seungone Kim, Bill Yuchen Lin, et al.
summary: Frames personalization as multi-objective RL (RLPHF): trains separate policies or reward signals per preference dimension and composes them at inference by post-hoc parameter merging, so each user's combination of preferences can be served without retraining.
relation: Composing per-dimension policies is a way to represent a user's preferences; the open question is whether interaction-policy dimensions (ask vs. act, confirm thresholds) can be merged the same way and inferred from behavior rather than declared.

title: Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback
authors: Long Ouyang et al.
summary: InstructGPT fine-tunes GPT-3 in three steps: supervised learning on labeler demonstrations, a reward model trained on labeler rankings, and PPO against that reward model, with a pretraining-mix variant (PPO-ptx) to reduce regressions. Labelers prefer the 1.3B InstructGPT to the 175B GPT-3. Truthfulness improves and toxicity falls when the model is prompted to be respectful, but bias does not improve. Alignment is to an aggregate of about 40 contracted labelers and researchers, not to individual users. The model is single-turn, learns no interaction policy, and does not adapt over time. The authors discuss group-conditioned preferences only as future work. It is useful as the outcome-averaged baseline for USIL.
relation: Canonical averaged-outcome alignment (the averaged/outcome cell of the 2x2).

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences
authors: Paul F. Christiano, Jan Leike, Tom B. Brown, Miljan Martic, Shane Legg, Dario Amodei
summary: Learns a reward model from pairwise human preference comparisons to train RL agents without hand-specified rewards.
relation: Foundation of preference learning; aggregates across labelers, so the per-user and procedural dimensions USIL targets are absent.

title: Ask Early, Ask Late, Ask Right: When Does Clarification Timing Matter for Long-Horizon Agents?
authors: Anmol Gulati, Hariom Gupta, Elias Lumer, et al.
summary: Injects ground-truth clarifications at controlled points in long-horizon agent trajectories across four information types (goal, input, constraint, context), finding that value depends strongly on timing and type (goal clarification nearly worthless after ~10% of execution; late clarification can be worse than none) and that current models over-ask or never ask.
relation: Adds the timing dimension to when-to-ask in agentic workflows; open question is whether optimal timing also varies by user (e.g., users who prefer upfront specification vs. mid-task check-ins) and can be learned.

title: Value of Information: A Framework for Human–Agent Communication
authors: Yijiang River Dong, Tiancheng Hu, Zheng Hui, Caiqi Zhang, Ivan Vulić, Andreea Bobu, Nigel Collier
summary: The paper proposes a decision-theoretic, inference-time Value of Information framework for LLM agents deciding whether to ask a clarifying question or act on an underspecified request. The LLM estimates a belief over latent user intent, simulates the answers to candidate questions, and asks only when expected utility gain exceeds the communication cost. It needs no threshold tuning. Across 20 Questions, flight preference, and ambiguous WebShop, with GPT-4.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash, VoI matches or beats tuned baselines in 18 of 20 conditions, but trails at higher costs. Users are simulated, and adaptation is limited to a single dialogue. It is a strong population-level procedural baseline for USIL.
relation: Principled when-to-ask rule with population-level costs; per-user costs are the USIL gap.

title: When Users Change Their Mind: Evaluating Interruptible Agents in Long-Horizon Web Navigation
authors: Henry Peng Zou, Chunyu Miao, Wei-Chieh Huang, et al.
decisions: Act or delegate;Intervene or take over;Defer or return control
summary: Introduces InterruptBench (from WebArena-Lite) with three interruption types (addition, revision, retraction) mid-execution, evaluating how well six LLM agents adapt to updated goals and recover efficiently; finds interruption handling remains hard for strong models.
relation: Treats interruptions as a feedback type agents must handle within a task; open question is whether interruption patterns can be learned as user evidence to anticipate a user's changes or to confirm earlier.

title: CollabLLM: From Passive Responders to Active Collaborators
authors: Shirley Wu, Michel Galley, Baolin Peng, et al.
decisions: Ask or clarify;Suggest;Intervene or take over
summary: CollabLLM trains LLMs to be active collaborators in multiturn dialogue. It estimates Multiturn-aware Rewards by simulating future turns with an LLM user simulator, then fine-tunes Llama-3.1-8B with SFT, DPO, or PPO. The resulting policy asks clarifying questions and makes suggestions when requests are ambiguous. In simulation it improves task performance by 18.5%, interactivity by 46.3%, and efficiency by 13.3%. A 201-person user study shows 17.6% higher satisfaction and 10.4% less time spent. Zero-shot transfer to Abg-CoQA shows more clarification. It does no per-user personalization or cross-session adaptation, and the authors list personalization as future work.
relation: Learns a population-level when-to-ask/suggest policy via long-horizon reward; open question is whether the multiturn-aware reward can be conditioned on an individual user's history so that clarification frequency adapts per user.

title: Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models
authors: Belinda Z. Li, Alex Tamkin, Noah Goodman, Jacob Andreas
summary: The paper introduces Generative Active Task Elicitation (GATE). Instead of users writing prompts or labeling examples, a language model interviews them with open-ended questions, yes/no questions or generated edge cases for five minutes. A GPT-4 predictor conditioned on the transcript then predicts that user's labels. Across content recommendation, moral reasoning and email validation, GATE often beats user-written prompts, supervised learning and pool-based active learning, with equal or lower reported mental effort. No model is trained, the question policy is prompt-only, and adaptation is single-session. It is a close predecessor for per-user elicitation but targets output preferences, not interaction procedure.
relation: Active elicitation per user; question budget and per-user cost of asking are open.

title: Learning to Clarify: Multi-turn Conversations with Action-Based Contrastive Self-Training
authors: Maximillian Chen, Ruoxi Sun, Tomas Pfister, Sercan Ö. Arık
summary: Proposes ACT, a quasi-online DPO variant that contrasts dialogue actions (clarify vs. answer) using on-policy multi-turn rollouts with a user simulator, learning data-efficient clarification policies; introduces AmbigSQL and evaluates on tabular QA and reading comprehension.
relation: Shows that action-level preference learning can shape ask-vs-act from little data, a natural mechanism for few-shot user adaptation; untested whether per-user action preferences (from approvals/rejections) can be learned the same way.

title: Modeling Future Conversation Turns to Teach LLMs to Ask Clarifying Questions
authors: Michael J. Q. Zhang, W. Bradley Knox, Eunsol Choi
summary: The paper teaches LLMs (Llama2, Gemma, Llama3) to ask clarifying questions for ambiguous QA by labeling DPO preferences through simulated future turns. A user simulator answers the clarifying question, and the downstream answer's F1 against each interpretation's gold answer decides whether asking or answering directly is preferred. This double-turn labeling gives about 5% higher F1 than single-turn preferences. A clarify-or-direct model also learns when clarification is needed and beats a random baseline. Users are simulated from dataset annotations, interactions last at most two turns, and there is no cross-session or per-user adaptation. Transfer to other tasks is left as future work.
relation: Directly tackles when-to-ask via future-turn credit assignment; remaining question is how to make the ask/answer threshold user-specific (some users prefer guesses, others prefer questions) from sparse feedback.

title: Structured Uncertainty guided Clarification for LLM Agents
authors: Manan Suri, Puneet Mathur, Nedim Lipka, et al.
summary: Models uncertainty over tool parameters and values and scores candidate clarifying questions by Expected Value of Perfect Information with a redundancy cost (SAGE-Agent), asking fewer questions with better coverage; uses the uncertainty as an RL (GRPO) signal and introduces ClarifyBench for multi-turn tool-calling disambiguation.
relation: Operationalizes value-of-information for agent clarification with an explicit question cost; open question is learning a user-specific question cost and prior over parameter values from that user's past answers.

title: Bayesian Preference Elicitation with Language Models
authors: Kunal Handa, Yarin Gal, Ellie Pavlick, et al.
summary: Proposes OPEN, combining Bayesian optimal experimental design (to choose the most informative query over LM-extracted features) with an LM that verbalizes queries in natural language; user studies show better preference elicitation than LM-only or BOED-only baselines.
relation: Principled information-gain question selection with an explicit per-user posterior; open question is extending the posterior to interaction preferences (not just item preferences) and deciding when the information is worth the user's effort.

title: Introspective Planning: Aligning Robots' Uncertainty with Inherent Task Ambiguity
authors: Kaiqu Liang, Zixu Zhang, Jaime Fernández Fisac
summary: Robots introspect over uncertainty to decide when to ask for clarification, with conformal guarantees.
relation: Calibrated asking under ambiguity; thresholds are not user-specific.

title: STaR-GATE: Teaching Language Models to Ask Clarifying Questions
authors: Chinmaya Andukuri, Jan-Philipp Fränken, Tobias Gerstenberg, Noah D. Goodman
summary: Self-improvement loop that trains LMs to ask useful clarifying questions with simulated users.
relation: Learns to ask well, but for a population of simulated users.

title: Tell Me More! Towards Implicit User Intention Understanding of Language Model Driven Agents
authors: Cheng Qian, Bingxiang He, Zhong Zhuang, et al.
summary: Introduces the Intention-in-Interaction (IN3) benchmark for detecting vague agent tasks and eliciting implicit user intentions through explicit questions, and trains Mistral-Interact as an upstream module that judges vagueness, queries missing details, and summarizes intent into goals before XAgent executes.
relation: Agent-level intent clarification before execution, elicited per task; open question is whether intentions elicited from a user can be stored and reused so future tasks need fewer questions.

title: Robots That Ask for Help: Uncertainty Alignment for Large Language Model Planners
authors: Allen Z. Ren et al.
summary: KnowNo: conformal prediction lets LLM planners ask for help when uncertain with statistical guarantees.
relation: Population-level help-seeking; USIL asks how coverage levels should vary by user.

title: A preference elicitation framework for automated planning
summary: Low-burden preference queries transfer to larger plans
relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P2; capabilities require full-text verification.

title: Unified Learning from Demonstrations, Corrections, and Preferences during Physical Human-Robot Interaction
summary: Integrates heterogeneous forms of robot teaching feedback
relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P2; capabilities require full-text verification.

title: Active Preference-Based Learning of Reward Functions
authors: Dorsa Sadigh, Anca D. Dragan, S. Shankar Sastry, Sanjit A. Seshia
summary: Actively selects comparison queries to learn a human's reward function efficiently.
relation: Query-efficient per-person learning; outcome rewards rather than interaction preferences.

title: KnowU-Bench: Towards Interactive, Proactive, and Personalized Mobile Agent Evaluation
authors: Tongbo Chen, Zhengxi Lu, Zhan Xu, et al.
decisions: Ask or clarify;Confirm;Intervene or take over;Defer or return control
summary: KnowU-Bench is an online Android-emulator benchmark for interactive, proactive, and personalized mobile agents, with 42 general, 86 personalized, and 64 proactive tasks. A hidden-profile LLM user simulator (gpt-4o) supplies clarification answers and consent or rejection. Agents see only timestamped behavior logs, clean or noisy, and must infer preferences or ask. In proactive tasks they choose between acting, proposing, and staying silent, and must stop after rejection. Hybrid rule and LLM-judge scoring is used. Of 11 models, Claude Sonnet 4.6 is best (60.4% SR), but hard personalized tasks peak at 44.2%. Failures are mostly poor clarification and miscalibrated intervention. No learning or temporal adaptation is studied.
relation: Directly evaluates per-user ask/intervene/consent decisions from inferred preferences, which makes it a candidate P4 testbed; it remains open whether agents improve these decisions over repeated sessions with the same user.

title: Latent Preference Modeling for Multi-Session Personalized Tool Calling
authors: Yejin Yoon, Minseo Kim, Taeuk Kim
summary: Introduces MPT, a benchmark of 4,695 instances from 459 multi-session histories that tests preference recall, inference and transfer when users leave out tool arguments, and PRefine, a test-time memory that keeps a textual hypothesis of latent user preferences and refines it with a generate-verify-refine loop; PRefine beats existing memory systems and full-history prompting on transfer.
relation: Shows that distilling history into preference hypotheses transfers better than raw memory, which is an argument for P2-style representations; it covers what to infer but not when inference is uncertain enough that the agent should ask instead.

title: Learning Next Action Predictors from Human-Computer Interaction
authors: Omar Shaikh et al.
summary: Trains models to predict a user's next action from interaction traces.
relation: Predicting what a user will do differs from learning how the user wants the agent to behave.

title: Toward Personalized LLM-Powered Agents: Foundations, Evaluation, and Future Directions
authors: Yue Xu, Qian Chen, Zizhan Ma, et al.
summary: A survey that organizes work on personalized LLM agents around four capabilities (profile modeling, memory, planning, action execution), analyzes how user signals move through the agent pipeline, and reviews metrics, benchmarks and applications.
relation: The most current map of personalized-agent work, useful for positioning; its taxonomy centers on profile, memory, planning and action content, and has no dedicated slot for personalizing the interaction policy (ask/act/defer).

title: User Preference Modeling for Conversational LLM Agents: Weak Rewards from Retrieval-Augmented Interaction
authors: Yuren Hao, Shuhaib Mehri, ChengXiang Zhai, Dilek Hakkani-Tür
summary: Proposes VARS, a frozen-backbone method that keeps a long-term and a short-term vector per user in a shared preference space, uses them to steer retrieval from structured preference memory, and updates them online from weak scalar feedback; on MultiSessionCollab it matches a strong reflection baseline on task success while reducing timeouts and user effort.
relation: Online per-user latent vectors updated from sparse feedback across sessions closely match USIL P1/P2; the open question is whether such vectors can condition interaction decisions (ask vs. act) rather than only memory retrieval.

title: Creating General User Models from Computer Use
authors: Omar Shaikh, Shardul Sapkota, Shan Rizvi, Eric Horvitz, Joon Sung Park, Diyi Yang, Michael S. Bernstein
summary: The paper presents General User Models (GUMs): per-user collections of natural-language, confidence-weighted propositions learned from unstructured computer observations (screenshots, notifications, emails) by prompting off-the-shelf LLMs and VLMs. A Propose, Retrieve, Revise, Audit pipeline updates propositions over time with decay scores. Applications query the GUM, including Gumbo, a proactive assistant that uses an expected-utility rule and rate limiting to decide when to interrupt. An email study (N=18) shows retrieval and revision improve win rate and calibration; a five-day Gumbo deployment (N=5) gives 0.79 accuracy, though only 25% of suggestions were rated strong or excellent. Cross-application transfer is claimed but not systematically tested.
relation: Rich persistent user model; how such a model should drive ask/act decisions is open.

title: Know Me, Respond to Me: Benchmarking LLMs for Dynamic User Profiling and Personalized Responses at Scale
authors: Bowen Jiang, Zhuoqun Hao, Young-Min Cho, et al. (incl. Lyle Ungar, Camillo J. Taylor, Dan Roth)
summary: PERSONAMEM is a benchmark of 20 synthetic personas with over 180 multi-session user-chatbot histories (up to 1M tokens), generated with GPT-4o. Seven in-situ query types test recalling facts, tracking evolving preferences, and generalizing to new scenarios. Models choose among four candidate responses. Fifteen LLMs reach only about 50% accuracy, struggle to incorporate the user's latest state, and do poorly on new scenarios. Reasoning models show no clear advantage. RAG and Mem0 improve accuracy, with RAG usually better. The benchmark is individual-level and longitudinal, but it covers output personalization only and has no interaction decisions such as asking or deferring.
relation: Provides an evaluation design for preference drift across sessions (P1), but only for response content; an analogous benchmark for drifting interaction preferences, such as a growing tolerance for autonomy, does not exist.

title: Large Language Models Empowered Personalized Web Agents
authors: Hongru Cai, Yongqi Li, Wenjie Wang, Fengbin Zhu, Xiaoyu Shen, Wenjie Li, Tat-Seng Chua
summary: Formulates LLM-empowered personalized web agents, releases the PersonalWAB benchmark (three personalized web tasks, single-turn and multi-turn evaluation with simulated users built from user profiles and behavior histories), and proposes PUMA, which retrieves relevant past behaviors from a memory bank and aligns the agent through SFT and DPO.
relation: A standard benchmark for personalizing what a web agent does from user history, but personalization targets action content rather than the interaction policy (when to ask or confirm).

title: PersonaAgent: Bridging Memory and Action for Personalized LLM Agents
authors: Weizhi Zhang, Xinyang Zhang, Chenwei Zhang, et al.
venue: NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Multi-Turn Interactions in LLMs (as 'PersonaAgent: When Large Language Model Agents Meet Personalization at Test Time'); arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.06254
summary: Presents a personalized agent framework with episodic and semantic memory and a personalized action (tool) module, linked by a per-user persona prompt that is refined at test time by simulating the user's recent interactions and applying textual-loss feedback.
relation: Test-time optimization of a textual per-user persona prompt is a candidate representation for pi_u, but it is evaluated on output and action personalization rather than on interaction decisions.

title: Personalization of Large Language Models: A Survey
authors: Zhehao Zhang et al.
summary: Survey and taxonomy of LLM personalization methods, data, and evaluation.
relation: Covers outcome personalization comprehensively; useful to show the procedural dimension is underrepresented.

title: Robust AI Personalization Will Require a Human Context Protocol
authors: Anand Shah, Tobin South, Talfan Evans, Hannah Rose Kirk, Andrew Trask, E. Glen Weyl, Michiel A. Bakker
summary: Position: personalization should rest on a user-owned, portable, natural-language preference layer shared across AI services.
relation: Portable user context is a representation locus for USIL; open question is whether stated preferences suffice for interaction decisions.

title: TidyBot: Personalized Robot Assistance with Large Language Models
authors: Jimmy Wu, Rika Antonova, Adam Kan, et al. (incl. Shuran Song, Jeannette Bohg, Thomas Funkhouser)
summary: A household robot infers a user's general object-placement rules by having an LLM summarize a few example placements, and these rules generalize to unseen objects (91.2% on the benchmark, 85% of objects put away in real-world tests).
relation: Canonical example of few-shot preference summarization that generalizes to new instances; USIL would apply the same summarize-and-generalize idea to procedural and interaction preferences instead of task outcomes.

title: User profiling and behavioral adaptation for HRI: A survey
summary: Survey of adapting robot physical cognitive social behavior based on user models
relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P2;P3; capabilities require full-text verification.

title: User–interface agent interaction: personalization issues
authors: Silvia Schiaffino, Analía Amandi
summary: This 2004 IJHCS paper reports a questionnaire survey of 42 users with varying expertise on interface agents, using the authors' agents or MS Office assistants. It examines which user–agent interaction issues need personalization in mixed-initiative settings: assistant type, allowed assistance actions, interruptions, error tolerance, feedback and autonomy. Preferences are heterogeneous. Only 12% want a collaborative agent, 49% allow suggestions but not autonomous action, and tolerance for errors and willingness to give feedback decline over time. The authors derive eight lessons and propose a user interaction profile of situation–action pairs with probabilities. No system is built, learned or evaluated; the profiling algorithms are future work.
relation: Earliest direct predecessor of USIL's interaction-policy framing; pre-LLM and rule/learning-based—how does it scale to tool-using LLM agents?

title: Learning and Reasoning about Interruption
summary: Direct old precedent learning per-user interruption costs and decisions
relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P3; capabilities require full-text verification.

title: Agents that Reduce Work and Information Overload
authors: Pattie Maes
summary: Foundational learning interface agents; slightly before the requested 1995 boundary
relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P2; capabilities require full-text verification.

title: AutoLibra: Agent Metric Induction from Open-Ended Human Feedback
authors: Hao Zhu, Phil Cuvin, Xinkai Yu, Charlotte Ka Yee Yan, Jason Zhang, Diyi Yang
summary: Induces agent evaluation metrics from open-ended human feedback.
relation: Feedback-derived metrics could be induced per user.

title: CollabSkill: Evaluating Human-Agent Collaboration on Real-World Tasks
authors: Yijia Shao, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Neel Ahuja, Yicheng Wang, Bowen Liu, Diyi Yang
summary: Benchmark of collaboration skills of agents on real-world tasks with humans.
relation: Collaboration metrics without individual adaptation.

title: Offloading Score: Measuring AI Reliance Through Counterfactual Workflows
authors: Vishakh Padmakumar, Lujain Ibrahim, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Jennifer Wang, Q. Vera Liao, Diyi Yang
summary: Measures how much users offload work to AI using counterfactual workflows.
relation: A reliance metric that could be computed per user.

title: Personalized Benchmarking: Evaluating LLMs by Individual Preferences
authors: Cristina Garbacea, Heran Wang, Chenhao Tan
summary: The paper introduces personalized benchmarking for LLMs. Using Chatbot Arena votes from 115 users with at least 25 battles, it computes per-user ELO and Bradley-Terry rankings over 20 models and finds that they diverge from global rankings (mean Spearman 0.432 for ELO, 0.043 for BT). Users also differ in query topics and writing style. A regression on topic and style features predicts user-specific rankings better than a mean-predictor baseline that mimics an aggregate benchmark (MAE reduced by 35% for ELO and 12% for BT). It studies no interaction decisions, temporal adaptation or transfer, and the validation set is small (18 users). It is correlational.
relation: Evidence that averaged evaluation misrepresents individuals—extends naturally to interaction behavior.

title: PrefIx: Understand and Adapt to User Preference in Human-Agent Interaction
authors: Jialin Li, Zhenhao Chen, Hanjun Luo, Hanan Salam
summary: PrefIx is a configurable simulation environment for evaluating how LLM agents interact, not just what they accomplish. Its Interaction-as-a-Tool paradigm casts interaction behaviors (confirmation, narration, clarification, error handling) as structured tool calls. A taxonomy of 14 preference attributes (31 settings) drives a preference-guided user simulator that expresses preferences only implicitly. Seven UX dimensions and preference alignment are scored by a validated multi-LLM-judge ensemble. Prompting four LLMs to infer preferences from a sample history improved UX by 7.6% and alignment by 18.5% on average, while generally preserving tool accuracy. Nothing is trained, and long-term adaptation, transfer and real users are not tested.
relation: One of the closest predecessors (interaction preferences); check whether adaptation is longitudinal.

title: RealWebAssist: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Web Assistance with Real-World Users
authors: Suyu Ye, Haojun Shi, Darren Shih, Hyokun Yun, Tanya Roosta, Tianmin Shu
summary: Benchmark of sequences of real users' instructions to a web assistant over extended multi-website interactions, requiring agents to infer intent, track changing mental state, learn user-specific routines, and ground instructions; state-of-the-art models struggle.
relation: Uses real users and requires learning personal routines over a long horizon; open question is evaluating whether agents use that accumulated evidence to change how they interact (ask less, act more) rather than just what they click.

title: Do LLMs Recognize Your Preferences? Evaluating Personalized Preference Following in LLMs
authors: Siyan Zhao et al.
summary: PrefEval benchmark for following stated user preferences across long conversations.
relation: Output-preference following; interaction decisions not evaluated.

title: PersonaLens: A Benchmark for Personalization Evaluation in Conversational AI Assistants
authors: Zheng Zhao, Clara Vania, Subhradeep Kayal, Naila Khan, Shay B. Cohen, Emine Yilmaz
summary: Builds a benchmark for personalization in task-oriented assistants using diverse user profiles with preferences and interaction histories, an LLM user agent that conducts realistic task dialogues, and an LLM judge that scores personalization, response quality, and task success.
relation: Combines user simulation with per-user profiles and separates personalization from task success; open question is adding judges for interaction-policy fit (did the assistant ask/confirm as this user prefers).

title: PersonalLLM: Tailoring LLMs to Individual Preferences
authors: Thomas P. Zollo et al.
summary: Benchmark with simulated heterogeneous users for personalization algorithms.
relation: Heterogeneous-user benchmark for outputs; template for an interaction-policy analogue.

title: SimulatorArena: Are User Simulators Reliable Proxies for Multi-Turn Evaluation of AI Assistants?
authors: Yao Dou, Michel Galley, Baolin Peng, et al.
summary: Collects 909 annotated human-LLM conversations (math tutoring, document creation) to test whether LLM user simulators reproduce human messages and human ratings; profile-conditioned simulators (background, communication style) reach Spearman rho about 0.7 with human judgments, and are used to benchmark 18 assistants.
relation: Directly addresses the validity of simulator-based evaluation that USIL benchmarks rely on; open question is whether profile-conditioned simulators also reproduce user-specific interaction behaviors (interruptions, corrections, takeovers), not just message style and ratings.

title: UserBench: An Interactive Gym Environment for User-Centric Agents
authors: Cheng Qian, Zuxin Liu, Akshara Prabhakar, et al.
summary: Gym environment in which simulated users start with vague goals and reveal preferences incrementally and implicitly, so tool-using agents must ask clarifying questions; finds that answers fully satisfy user intent only ~20% of the time and top models elicit under 30% of preferences.
relation: Separates task completion from preference alignment and measures elicitation, but each episode is a fresh user; open question is whether agents can learn across episodes which users need to be asked and which can be inferred.

title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
authors: Shunyu Yao, Noah Shinn, Pedram Razavi, Karthik Narasimhan
summary: τ-bench is a benchmark for tool-agent-user interaction in retail and airline domains. An LM simulates a human user with a task instruction, the agent has domain APIs and a policy document, and success is judged by comparing the final database state with an annotated goal state. The paper introduces pass^k, the probability that all k i.i.d. trials succeed, to measure reliability. Twelve LMs are tested with function calling, ReAct and Act. The best, gpt-4o, reaches 61.2% pass^1 in retail and 35.2% in airline, with pass^8 below 25% in retail. Nothing is learned and there is no personalization or longitudinal adaptation, but it is a useful procedural evaluation baseline.
relation: Task-success evaluation with users in the loop, but no per-user adaptation.

title: LaMP: When Large Language Models Meet Personalization
authors: Alireza Salemi, Sheshera Mysore, Michael Bendersky, Hamed Zamani
summary: Introduces LaMP, a seven-task benchmark (3 classification, 4 generation) where each example is tied to a user profile, and evaluates retrieval-augmented personalization that pulls items from the user's history into the prompt.
relation: Canonical per-user benchmark, but it scores personalized outputs only; it leaves open how to benchmark user-specific interaction decisions (ask/act/confirm) conditioned on the same kind of history.

title: WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents
authors: Shuyan Zhou et al.
summary: Realistic web environment benchmark for autonomous agents.
relation: Canonical task-success benchmark (contrast case).

title: Appropriate Reliance on AI Advice: Conceptualization and the Effect of Explanations
summary: Appropriate reliance definition and human-centered evaluation
relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P4; capabilities require full-text verification.

title: Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback
authors: Kaiqu Liang, Julia Kruk, Shengyi Qian, Xianjun Yang, Shengjie Bi, Yuanshun Yao, Shaoliang Nie, Mingyang Zhang, Lijuan Liu, Jaime Fernández Fisac, Shuyan Zhou, Saghar Hosseini
summary: PAHF (Personalized Agents from Human Feedback) is a continual personalization framework in which a prompted LLM agent learns per-user natural-language preference notes in isolated external memory. It combines proactive pre-action clarification, asked when an instruction is ambiguous and memory lacks relevant information, with reactive post-action feedback that revises memory under preference drift. A four-phase protocol on new embodied-manipulation and online-shopping benchmarks uses simulated personas. PAHF beats No Memory, Pre-action Only and Post-action Only baselines in all phases, and Pre-action Only collapses after drift. Transfer is tested only within a persona, and feedback is simulated and noise-free.
relation: Very close to USIL (clarification + memory + feedback); open question is learning a per-user policy for when to ask, not only what to remember.

title: MemToolAgent: Leveraging Memory for Tool Using Agents Based on Environment and User Feedback
authors: Suleyman Armagan Er, Danilo Ribeiro, Yogesh Virkar, et al.
summary: A fine-tuning-free memory framework for tool-using agents. It uses a unified memory-entry format and reflection that turns failed executions, together with environment and user feedback, into stored critiques. Retrieval sets how many past experiences to use from the similarity distribution of stored memories. Reports gains on WorkBench, NESTFUL and PEToolBench, including personalized tool use.
relation: Among the closest memory systems to USIL, because it writes user feedback into reusable critiques that change later agent behaviour; open question: whether per-user feedback memories generalize across tasks and shape ask-vs-act decisions, not only tool-call correctness.

title: MultiSessionCollab: Learning User Preferences with Memory to Improve Long-Term Collaboration
authors: Shuhaib Mehri, Priyanka Kargupta, Tal August, Dilek Hakkani-Tür
summary: MultiSessionCollab is a benchmark for long-term collaboration in which user simulators with personas and three interaction preferences each work with an agent over 20 sessions. The agent keeps a reflective natural-language memory of user preferences, contexts and satisfying strategies, and the reflection policy is trained with GRPO using rewards from simulator behavior. Memory improves task success and reduces user effort and conversation length versus no memory, Mem0 and history baselines, and approaches an oracle. A 19-participant study corroborates the gains but shows weaker cross-domain generalization. Preferences are explicit and static, and ask/act/defer decisions are neither learned nor evaluated.
relation: One of the closest predecessors; remaining question is explicit ask/act/defer decisions and transfer across tasks.

title: VitaBench 2.0: Evaluating Personalized and Proactive Agents in Long-Term User Interactions
authors: Yuxin Chen, Yi Zhang, Zhengzhou Cai, et al.
summary: VitaBench 2.0 is a benchmark of temporally ordered tool-use task sequences for 56 synthetic users with over 2,000 preferences, three domains (Delivery, In-store, OTA) and 66 tools. Preferences drift between tasks, and histories are fragmented and noisy. Some tasks are proactive, so the agent must ask or explore to fill in missing context. An UPDATE/RETRIEVE memory interface compares full context, agentic memory and RAG across about 25 LLM configurations. The best model reaches Avg@4 of about 0.5 and Pass^4 of about 0.3. Memory usually hurts, performance degrades over the sequence, and proactive scores trail personalization scores. Nothing is trained and transfer is not tested.
relation: Combines longitudinal per-user memory with ask-vs-infer evaluation, close to the USIL evaluation setting; open question: does it score whether the agent's asking behaviour adapts to the individual user (asking less once preferences are known), rather than gathering information uniformly?

title: Agent Workflow Memory
authors: Zora Zhiruo Wang, Jiayuan Mao, Daniel Fried, Graham Neubig
summary: AWM induces reusable workflows (common sub-routines) from past agent trajectories, offline from training examples or online from test queries, and supplies the relevant ones to guide later actions. Gives 24.6% and 51.1% relative success gains on Mind2Web and WebArena, with growing gains under cross-task, cross-website and cross-domain shift.
relation: The canonical procedural-memory mechanism, which could hold user-specific routines (which steps a user lets the agent run autonomously); open question: inducing workflows from one user's demonstrations and takeovers, annotated with where the user wants checkpoints.

title: In Prospect and Retrospect: Reflective Memory Management for Long-term Personalized Dialogue Agents
authors: Zhen Tan, Jun Yan, I-Hung Hsu, et al.
summary: Reflective Memory Management (RMM) builds a personalized memory bank by summarizing interactions at the utterance, turn and session levels (prospective reflection). It then refines retrieval with online RL, using the evidence the LLM cites as the signal (retrospective reflection). Reports more than 10% accuracy gain over a no-memory baseline on LongMemEval.
relation: Online learning of what to retrieve resembles adapting a per-user memory policy from sparse signals; open question: could the RL signal be real user reactions (accept, edit, interrupt) instead of self-citations, and could it drive interaction decisions?

title: LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory
authors: Di Wu, Hongwei Wang, Wenhao Yu, Yuwei Zhang, Kai-Wei Chang, Dong Yu
summary: A 500-question benchmark embedded in scalable user-assistant histories. It tests information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates and abstention, and shows about a 30% accuracy drop for commercial assistants and long-context LLMs. Proposes an indexing/retrieval/reading decomposition of memory design with optimizations such as session decomposition and time-aware query expansion.
relation: The knowledge-update and abstention axes map onto preference drift (P1) and deference (P3), but only for factual recall; open question: does updated memory change downstream interaction choices (for example, stop asking once a preference is known)?

title: Memp: Exploring Agent Procedural Memory
authors: Runnan Fang, Yuan Liang, Xiaobin Wang, et al.
summary: Distills past agent trajectories into a learnable, lifelong procedural memory with step-level instructions and script-like abstractions. Studies strategies for building, retrieving and updating it (including correcting and deprecating outdated entries) and shows gains on TravelPlanner and ALFWorld, plus transfer of memory from stronger to weaker models.
relation: Its update, correct and deprecate operations are a template for maintaining evolving procedural preferences under drift; open question: procedural memory keyed to a user, updated from that user's corrections instead of task-success signals.

title: Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents
authors: Adyasha Maharana, Dong-Ho Lee, Sergey Tulyakov, Mohit Bansal, Francesco Barbieri, Yuwei Fang
summary: Introduces LoCoMo: very long multi-session dialogues (about 300 turns and 9K tokens, up to 35 sessions) generated by persona- and event-graph-grounded LLM agents, then human-verified. Benchmarks QA, event summarization and multimodal dialogue generation, and finds that LLMs and RAG lag far behind humans on long-range temporal and causal reasoning.
relation: The standard longitudinal memory benchmark, but it tests recall of conversational facts rather than whether remembered evidence changes the agent's ask/act behaviour; open question: an analogous long-horizon benchmark whose targets are interaction decisions.

title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
authors: Charles Packer, Sarah Wooders, Kevin Lin, et al.
summary: Proposes virtual context management, inspired by OS memory hierarchies: the LLM manages tiered memory (in-context vs. external) through function calls and interrupts. Evaluated on large-document analysis and multi-session chat, where the agent keeps and builds on user information across sessions.
relation: Supplies the architecture for persistent per-user state that a pi_u could condition on, but stores what users said rather than how they want the agent to interact; open question: what memory schema captures interaction-policy evidence such as takeovers and rejections?

title: Collaborative Interface Agents
authors: Yezdi Lashkari; Max Metral; Pattie Maes
summary: Learns patterns from user activity and transfers knowledge across agents; slightly before period
relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P2; capabilities require full-text verification.

title: Getting Better at Working With You: Compiling User Corrections into Runtime Enforcement for Coding Agents
authors: Yujun Zhou, Kehan Guo, Haomin Zhuang, et al. (incl. Nitesh V. Chawla, Xiangliang Zhang)
summary: The paper identifies an access-compliance gap in coding agents: they can retrieve a user's remembered corrections and still violate them (compliance is 31.6% with no rules, 55.0% with all rules). Trace, a drop-in skill-layer pipeline, compiles chat corrections into a per-user library of atomic rules, each with an applicability check, a behavior instruction and a verifier. A lifecycle resolver maintains the library, and runtime hooks block task completion until active verifiers pass. On ClawArena and MemoryArena-derived tasks with simulated users, Trace lowers violations and user turns versus Mem0, Hindsight and ReMe-Light. OOD transfer is strong on ClawArena and weak on MemoryArena.
relation: Very close to USIL's 'tell once' goal for procedural preferences across tasks; open question is whether corrections about the interaction itself (ask less, confirm before X) can be compiled the same way, and how rules are retired when preferences drift.

title: Learning on the Job: Continual Learning from Deployment Feedback for Frozen-Weights Agents
authors: Valentin Tablan, Scott Taylor, Kristoffer Bernhem
summary: Pairs a frozen LLM agent with an external memory that distills each deployment episode into retrievable natural-language rules, learning from one-bit outcome verdicts or post-hoc corrections; on tau-bench banking, corrections give 2.6x the static-RAG baseline, and memory transfers across models.
relation: Shows continual learning without weight updates from cheap deployment feedback; the memory is shared across users, so per-user scoping and interaction-level rules remain open.

title: SPRInG: Continual LLM Personalization via Selective Parametric Adaptation and Retrieval-Interpolated Generation
authors: Seoyeon Kim, Jaehyung Kim
summary: Addresses user-interest drift in continual personalization: a likelihood-based novelty score detects genuine preference shifts and updates a user-specific adapter only then (with a replay buffer), and inference interpolates parametric outputs with gated retrieval over history.
relation: Directly tackles separating real drift from transient context in per-user continual updates; open question is whether drift-gated updates work for interaction-policy evidence, which is sparser and noisier.

title: Principled Fine-tuning of LLMs from User-Edits: A Medley of Preference, Supervision, and Reward
authors: Dipendra Misra, Aldo Pacchiano, Ta-Chung Chi, Ge Gao
summary: Treats deployment logs of (context, agent response, user edit) as a mix of preference, supervised, and cost feedback; derives learning bounds for each and proposes an ensembling procedure that learns from all three, adapting robustly to different user-edit distributions at test time (domains adapted from PRELUDE).
relation: Gives the theory for learning from edits, a core USIL evidence type; open question is whether edit cost can also train interaction decisions (for example, confirm before acting when expected edit cost is high).

title: Retrospective Learning from Interactions
authors: Zizhao Chen, Mustafa Omer Gul, Yiwei Chen, Gloria Geng, Anne Wu, Yoav Artzi
summary: Shows that implicit signals in multi-turn deployed interactions (rephrasing, frustration, switching tasks) are task-general and can be decoded retrospectively into rewards; ReSpect retrains the model over successive deployment rounds with thousands of real human interactions, raising task completion from 31% to 82%.
relation: Closest working example of continual learning from implicit in-deployment evidence; open question is whether the same retrospective decoding can be kept per user and applied to interaction decisions (e.g., when the user rephrases because the agent should have asked).

title: Right Now, Wrong Then: Non-Stationary Direct Preference Optimization under Preference Drift
authors: Seongho Son, William Bankes, Sayak Ray Chowdhury, Brooks Paige, Ilija Bogunovic
summary: Models time-varying preferences with a Dynamic Bradley-Terry model and proposes NS-DPO, which exponentially discounts older preference pairs; gives estimation-error and regret bounds under unknown drift and shows robustness when fine-tuning LLMs under drifting preferences.
relation: Gives a principled discounting approach for drift in preference evidence; open question is how to discount sparse per-user interaction evidence (e.g., takeovers) and tell real drift from context-dependent variation.

title: The Era of Real-World Human Interaction: RL from User Conversations
authors: Chuanyang Jin, Jing Xu, Bo Liu, et al. (incl. Tianmin Shu, Jason Weston)
venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2509.25137 (also an ICLR 2026 workshop poster)
summary: Proposes Reinforcement Learning from Human Interaction (RLHI), which learns from organic WildChat conversations through (i) user-guided rewrites that revise weak outputs using the user's follow-up message and (ii) persona-conditioned rewards built from each user's long-term interaction history; improves personalization and instruction following.
relation: Conditions a reward on each user's multi-session history built from natural follow-ups; it still learns output preferences rather than when to ask, confirm, or defer for that user.

title: Personalized Adaptation via In-Context Preference Learning
authors: Allison Lau, Younwoo Choi, Vahid Balazadeh, Keertana Chidambaram, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Rahul G. Krishnan
venue: NeurIPS 2024 Workshop on Adaptive Foundation Models; arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.14001
summary: Preference Pretrained Transformer (PPT) is trained offline with a history-dependent loss so that, online, it adapts to an individual user's preferences purely in context from that user's feedback; it outperforms per-user fine-tuning baselines in a contextual-bandit setting at much lower compute.
relation: A test-time adaptation recipe (meta-train offline, adapt in context) that could carry over to learning pi_u; still open whether it scales beyond bandit toys to multi-step interaction decisions.

title: Robot Learning on the Job: Human-in-the-Loop Autonomy and Learning During Deployment
authors: Huihan Liu, Soroush Nasiriany, Lance Zhang, Zhiyao Bao, Yuke Zhu
venue: Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS) 2023; arXiv preprint arXiv:2211.08416
decisions: Act or delegate;Intervene or take over;Defer or return control
summary: Sirius: a partially autonomous robot runs while a human monitors and takes over at hard moments; deployment data are reweighted by estimated human trust (from interventions) and used for weighted behavior cloning, improving the policy across deployment rounds.
relation: A foundational example of turning takeovers into learning signal and gradually shifting autonomy; open question is how to make this per user, since takeovers reflect individual trust and preference as well as policy failure.

title: Physical interaction as communication: Learning robot objectives online from human corrections
summary: Learns user task objectives online from corrections; useful distinction from learning procedure
relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P2; capabilities require full-text verification.

title: Learning from interventions: Human-robot interaction as both explicit and implicit feedback
summary: Treats interventions and non-interventions as evidence for robot learning
relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P3; capabilities require full-text verification.
